column31: The updated Energy Plan 2025 draws its baseline energy data from Johannesburg's 2023/24 electricity profile, which establishes total consumption at 9,758 GWh (9.76 million MWh). The City's electricity supply is dominated by purchases from Eskom (83%), with Eskom's generation portfolio nationally still heavily coal-dependent (about 73% coal). Locally, the Kelvin Power Station adds another 11.5% of supply, also coal-fired, while the remaining 4.5% comes from independent power producers (IPPs), rooftop solar, and small embedded generation projects.\nThe report also incorporates national-level energy data from the Integrated Resource Plan (IRP 2019 and draft 2023), the Electricity Regulation Amendment Act (2024), and the Climate Change Act (2024), which together frame South Africa's planned energy transition. For projections, the Roadmap uses modelling outputs from the Needs Analysis Report (2024) and scenarios that reflect national trends such as coal plant decommissioning, Eskom's grid composition, and renewable energy integration through the REIPPPP programme.\nIn addition, the Roadmap considers specific local initiatives—such as waste-to-energy plants, gas-to-power projects (e.g. John Ware and Durban Street stations), and rooftop solar PV growth—as part of Johannesburg's embedded generation capacity. Wheeling arrangements, particularly through the National Wheeling Framework (2023), also inform future renewable energy access by allowing the City to procure solar and wind power from resource-rich provinces.

Para o consumo total da jurisdição, foram utilizados dados disponíveis do município. Na decomposição percentual reportada, foram utilizados dados representativos da matriz elétrica brasileira. O percentual do consumo por tipo de energia foi reportado com base na matriz elétrica nacional, pois a cidade é abastecida pelo Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), que conecta diferentes regiões do país. Isso permite que São Paulo consuma energia gerada em outros estados, como de hidrelétricas, eólicas e outras fontes. O SIN garante a distribuição eficiente e estável de energia, independentemente da origem, tornando necessário que o consumo da cidade reflita a participação de todas as fontes da matriz elétrica nacional, e não apenas as do estado de São Paulo, onde a jurisdição está localizada. No detalhamento do consumo, não foi reportado o valor referente à energia proveniente de importação líquida, pois não é possível identificar a fonte específica de geração nesse processo.

The electricity consumption of Ankara Metropolitan Municipality (ABB) has been reported based on national-level data from the Turkish Electricity Transmission Corporation (TEİAŞ) for the year 2022, as jurisdiction-specific breakdown data is not publicly available. This approach is consistent with the methodology applied in the Ankara LCCAP (Local Climate Change Action Plan) and the YIDEP (Climate Change Adaptation and Emission Reduction Program), which both align with the Global Covenant of Mayors (GCoM) Common Reporting Framework requirements.

According to TEİAŞ data, the Turkish national electricity mix in 2022 consisted of approximately 31% coal, 22% natural gas, 1% oil, 3% nuclear, and 43% renewable sources. Within renewables, the largest contributors were hydropower (20%), wind (11%), solar (7%), geothermal (3%), and bioenergy (2%). Ankara's grid electricity consumption therefore reflects this national composition, as the city is fully integrated into the national transmission and distribution system.

Although the grid mix is defined nationally, ABB has undertaken significant efforts to increase the share of local renewable energy generation within the jurisdiction. The municipality has supported the installation of solar PV systems for rural irrigation, promoted rooftop PV applications in public buildings, and implemented biogas-to-energy recovery through the Mamak Integrated Solid Waste Facility (ITC), which captures methane emissions and generates electricity from landfill gas. These projects contribute directly to the renewable share of Ankara's electricity use and demonstrate the city's commitment to low-carbon development.

The inclusion of nuclear power (3%) reflects the initial contribution of the Akkuyu Nuclear Power Plant, which entered the Turkish grid mix. While nuclear energy is not renewable, it reduces dependency on fossil fuel imports and contributes to the diversification of the energy portfolio.

In addition to supply-side efforts, ABB promotes demand-side management by supporting energy efficiency measures in municipal facilities, advancing public transport electrification plans, and raising awareness on household energy savings. The combination of national grid decarbonization and local renewable deployment is critical to achieving the city's mitigation targets under GCoM and Turkey's National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP).

2023 national grid fuel mix data was available at the time of reporting, but the latest total energy consumption data for Brighton & Hove is from 2022, so for consistency between responses, we have used the national electricity fuel mix figures from 2022. In 2022, the UK exported more electricity than we imported so Net Imports are not included in the fuel mix we are reporting. When reporting “Other fuels” (2.1% of electricity generated in the UK in 2022) , the UK government does not distinguish between renewable sources (e.g. geothermal, wave, and tidal) and non-renewable (e.g. waste to energy) 'other fuels'. These are reported together with 'energy storage' (<1% of electricity consumed in the UK in 2022) as “other non-renewable fuels”. As such, the figures above likely slightly underestimate the share of renewables in the 2022 UK electricity mix. In 2024, renewable fuels accounted for a greater share of the total electricity fuel mix, as compared to 2022, and was the first year that renewables constituted more than 50% of electricity fuel mix in the UK.
